claim: Crown-group animals (metazoans) originated around 850 million years ago (Ma).
source: Crown-group animals (metazoans) originated around 850 million years ago (Ma) (Dohrmann and Wörheide, 2017)
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Dohrmann and Wörheide, 2017.

claim: Atmospheric oxygen was likely <10% of its present level around 850 million years ago.
source: when atmospheric oxygen (O2) was likely <10% of its present level (Lenton and Daines, 2017)
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Lenton and Daines, 2017.

claim: Less atmospheric oxygen would have led to extensive deep-ocean anoxia and high redox variability in marine surface waters.
source: Less atmospheric oxygen would had led to extensive deep-ocean anoxia and high redox variability in marine surface waters (Reinhard et al., 2016)
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Reinhard et al., 2016.

claim: Low oxygen environments place energetic constraints on the diversity, abundance, and physiology of heterotrophic eukaryotes, particularly animals.
source: thereby placing energetic constraints on the diversity, abundance, and physiology of heterotrophic eukaryotes, particularly animals (Fenchel and Finlay, 1995)
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Fenchel and Finlay, 1995.

claim: In all previously examined animal lineages, decreasing cellular oxygen concentrations alter gene expression via the hypoxia-inducible factor (HIF).
source: In all previously examined animal lineages, decreasing cellular oxygen concentrations, whether environmentally or metabolically driven, alter gene expression via the hypoxia-inducible factor (HIF), a key pathway for maintaining physiological oxygen homeostasis (Loenarz et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Loenarz et al., 2011.

claim: The HIF pathway consists of two bHLH-PAS-domain transcription factors (HIFa and HIFb/ARNT) that form a heterodimer to initiate transcription when oxygen concentrations at the cellular level are low.
source: The HIF pathway consists of two bHLH-PAS-domain transcription factors (HIFa and HIFb/ARNT) that form a heterodimer to initiate transcription when oxygen concentrations at the cellular level are low (Semenza, 2007).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Semenza, 2007.

claim: At higher oxygen levels, HIFa is hydroxylated by HPH (also called PHD or EGL9), a member of the 2-oxoglutarate-dependent oxygenase family.
source: At higher oxygen levels, HIFa is hydroxylated by a member of the 2-oxoglutarate-dependent oxygenase family, HPH (Bruick and McKnight, 2001), also called PHD or EGL9
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Bruick and McKnight, 2001.

claim: Hydroxylated HIFa is signaled for destruction by the von Hippel-Lindau (VHL) protein, thereby avoiding its dimerization with HIFb and subsequent transcriptional activation.
source: and is then signaled for destruction by the von Hippel-Lindau (VHL) protein, thereby avoiding its dimerization with HIFb and subsequent transcriptional activation (Min et al., 2002).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Min et al., 2002.

claim: Proteins in the HIF pathway have been characterized in many metazoan groups.
source: Proteins in the HIF pathway have been characterized in many metazoan groups (Kaelin and Ratcliffe, 2008)
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Kaelin and Ratcliffe, 2008.

claim: Proteins in the HIF pathway have been characterized in placozoans.
source: including placozoans (Loenarz et al., 2011)
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Loenarz et al., 2011.

claim: Proteins in the HIF pathway have been characterized in cnidarians.
source: and cnidarians (Wang et al., 2014)
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Wang et al., 2014.

claim: Proteins in the HIF pathway have not been evaluated in sponges (Phylum Porifera) and comb-jellies (Phylum Ctenophora).
source: but have not been evaluated in sponges (Phylum Porifera) and comb-jellies (Phylum Ctenophora)
evidence: The claim is explicitly stated in the text.

claim: Sponges and ctenophores are the two most likely candidates that have been discussed as the sister-lineage to all remaining animals.
source: the two most likely candidates that have been discussed as the sister-lineage to all remaining animals (e.g. King and Rokas, 2017), but see Simion et al. (2017); Feuda et al., 2017)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to King and Rokas, 2017, Simion et al., 2017, and Feuda et al., 2017.

claim: The demosponge Halichondria panicea can survive under 1.6–12.7 µM O2.
source: While previous experiments on the demosponge Halichondria panicea demonstrated survival under 1.6–12.7 µM O2 (Mills et al., 2014)
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Mills et al., 2014.

claim: No transcriptional data from sponges kept under low-oxygen have been reported.
source: no transcriptional data from sponges kept under low-oxygen have been reported (Mentel et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Mentel et al., 2014.

claim: It remains unclear whether the HIF pathway extends to all living animals.
source: Therefore, it remains unclear whether the HIF pathway extends to all living animals, which would parsimoniously suggest that HIF is an ancestral feature of animal life.
evidence: The claim is based on the lack of data on HIF in sponges and ctenophores.

claim: All animal groups have bHLH-PAS family proteins.
source: we found that all animal groups -- as well as the single-celled eukaryotic outgroup, Capsaspora owczarzaki (Suga et al., 2013) -- have bHLH-PAS family proteins (Figure 1a,b).
evidence: The claim is supported by comparative genomics data and a citation to Suga et al., 2013, as well as Figure 1a,b.

claim: The single-celled eukaryotic outgroup, Capsaspora owczarzaki, has bHLH-PAS family proteins.
source: we found that all animal groups -- as well as the single-celled eukaryotic outgroup, Capsaspora owczarzaki (Suga et al., 2013) -- have bHLH-PAS family proteins (Figure 1a,b).
evidence: The claim is supported by comparative genomics data and a citation to Suga et al., 2013, as well as Figure 1a,b.

claim: No members of the bHLH-PAS protein family were found in the genomes or transcriptomes of choanoflagellates.
source: No members of this protein family were found in the genomes or transcriptomes of choanoflagellates, the sister lineage to animals (King et al., 2008; Fairclough et al., 2013; Carr et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by comparative genomics data and citations to King et al., 2008, Fairclough et al., 2013, and Carr et al., 2017.

claim: Choanoflagellates are the sister lineage to animals.
source: the sister lineage to animals (King et al., 2008; Fairclough et al., 2013; Carr et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to King et al., 2008, Fairclough et al., 2013, and Carr et al., 2017.

claim: One-to-one orthologs of HIFa are found in cnidarians and placozoans.
source: While one-to-one orthologs of HIFa are found in cnidarians and placozoans, sponges and ctenophores lack true one-to-one HIFa orthologs (Figure 1a,b).
evidence: The claim is supported by comparative genomics data and Figure 1a,b.

claim: Sponges and ctenophores lack true one-to-one HIFa orthologs.
source: While one-to-one orthologs of HIFa are found in cnidarians and placozoans, sponges and ctenophores lack true one-to-one HIFa orthologs (Figure 1a,b).
evidence: The claim is supported by comparative genomics data and Figure 1a,b.

claim: Vertebrate HIF1a arose from a series of duplications that gave rise to HIFa, SIM1, SIM2, NPAS1 and NPAS3.
source: The phylogeny obtained for the bHLH-PAS family (Figure 2) reveals that vertebrate HIF1a arose from a series of duplications that gave rise to HIFa, SIM1, SIM2, NPAS1 and NPAS3
evidence: The claim is supported by phylogenetic analysis shown in Figure 2.

claim: The function of the ancestral bHLH-PAS protein is unclear.
source: and that the function of the ancestral protein is unclear (Figure 2).
evidence: The claim is based on phylogenetic analysis shown in Figure 2.

claim: The position of both sponge and ctenophore sequences in the phylogenetic tree suggests that sponge and ctenophore orthologs are sister to all HIF-SIM-NPAS (HSN) proteins.
source: The position of both sponge and ctenophore sequences in the tree suggests that sponge and ctenophore orthologs are sister to all HIF-SIM-NPAS (HSN) proteins
evidence: The claim is supported by phylogenetic analysis shown in Figure 2.

claim: The lack of one-to-one HIFa orthologs in sponges and ctenophores reflects the primary absence of HIFa in these phyla, rather than a secondary loss.
source: and that the lack of one-to-one HIFa orthologs reflects the primary absence of HIFa in these phyla, rather than a secondary loss.
evidence: The claim is based on phylogenetic inference from the tree topology.

claim: HIFa is hydroxylated at a key proline in the motif L[D/E]x[L/R]AP[F/Y]I in the presence of oxygen.
source: In the presence of oxygen, HIFa is hydroxylated at a key proline in the motif L[D/E]x[L/R]AP[F/Y]I that signals the protein for degradation.
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge of HIF pathway biochemistry.

claim: The hydroxylation motif varies between clades, where the LAPY motif in vertebrate HIFa is instead RAPY in most protostomes, RAPY or RAPF in cnidarians, and LAPF in placozoans.
source: The motif varies between clades, where the LAPY motif in vertebrate HIFa is instead RAPY in most protostomes, RAPY or RAPF in cnidarians, and LAPF in placozoans (Figure 3).
evidence: The claim is supported by sequence analysis shown in Figure 3.

claim: None of the hydroxylation motifs (LAPY, RAPY, RAPF, LAPF) were found in any of the sequences from the 26 sponge genomes and transcriptomes.
source: None of these motifs were found in any of the sequences from the 26 sponge genomes and transcriptomes in our set.
evidence: The claim is supported by sequence analysis of sponge genomes and transcriptomes.

claim: A similar motif (LAMRAPYI) was found in the C-terminal domain of a bHLH-PAS protein from the ctenophore Euplokamis dunlapae.
source: However, a similar motif (LAMRAPYI) was found in the C-terminal domain of a bHLH-PAS protein from the ctenophore Euplokamis dunlapae
evidence: The claim is supported by sequence analysis of ctenophore proteins.

claim: The LAMRAPYI motif was not found in any of the other eight ctenophores examined.
source: but not in any of the other eight ctenophores.
evidence: The claim is supported by sequence analysis of ctenophore proteins.

claim: The residues surrounding the LAMRAPYI motif in Euplokamis dunlapae do not align well with the ODD domains from HIFa in other animals.
source: The residues surrounding this motif do not align well with the ODD domains from HIFa in other animals, thus the role of this protein cannot be determined by this study.
evidence: The claim is based on sequence alignment analysis.

claim: The C-terminal domains of nearly all bHLH-PAS proteins are enriched for repeats of proline, serine, and glutamine.
source: The C-terminal domains of nearly all bHLH-PAS proteins are enriched for repeats of proline, serine, and glutamine, which makes them difficult to align and may cause downstream problems in tree generation.
evidence: The claim is based on sequence composition analysis.

claim: LAP or RAP motifs can be identified in many sponge sequences by chance due to the high abundance of prolines.
source: As prolines are highly abundant (Figure 3b), LAP or RAP motifs can be identified in many sponge sequences by chance
evidence: The claim is based on sequence analysis shown in Figure 3b.

claim: Proteins that are not known to have oxygen-dependent degradation, including human NPAS1 and NPAS3, contain LAP or RAP motifs.
source: but also proteins that are not known to have oxygen-dependent degradation, including human NPAS1 and NPAS3, suggesting that this short motif may occur without functional relevance.
evidence: The claim is based on sequence analysis and known protein functions.

claim: Prolines are mostly inflexible and rarely can be exchanged for other amino acids.
source: Additionally, prolines have a unique structural role in proteins as they are mostly inflexible, meaning they rarely can be exchanged for other amino acids.
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge of protein biochemistry.

claim: Alignment programs may cluster sequences around prolines, resulting in apparent alignments of non-homologous domains.
source: For this reason, alignment programs may cluster sequences around prolines, resulting in apparent alignments of non-homologous domains (Figure 3c,d).
evidence: The claim is based on understanding of alignment algorithms and is illustrated in Figure 3c,d.

claim: None of the sponge bHLH-PAS proteins are expected to function like HIFa because they do not have the full hydroxylation motif.
source: Since we do not find the full hydroxylation motif in any sponge bHLH-PAS protein, none of these proteins are expected to function like HIFa.
evidence: The claim is based on sequence analysis and inference about protein function.

claim: VHL orthologs were not found in any ctenophore or sponges outside of a few demosponges.
source: VHL orthologs were not found in any ctenophore or sponges outside of a few demosponges (Figure 1b, Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by comparative genomics data shown in Figure 1b and Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: EGL9/PHD orthologs were not found in any sponge or ctenophore.
source: We were also unable to find EGL9/PHD orthologs in any sponge or ctenophore, although we found related genes in microbial eukaryotes, including choanoflagellates (Figure 1b, Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by comparative genomics data shown in Figure 1b and Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: Related genes to EGL9/PHD were found in microbial eukaryotes, including choanoflagellates.
source: although we found related genes in microbial eukaryotes, including choanoflagellates (Figure 1b, Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by comparative genomics data shown in Figure 1b and Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: Homologs of the Factor Inhibiting HIF (FIH/HIF1AN) were identified in sponges.
source: We were, however, able to identify homologs of the Factor Inhibiting HIF (FIH/HIF1AN) in sponges (Figure 1b, Figure 2—figure supplement 3)
evidence: The claim is supported by comparative genomics data shown in Figure 1b and Figure 2—figure supplement 3.

claim: FIH/HIF1AN is a protein involved in regulation of HIF by hydroxylating C-terminal asparagines.
source: a protein involved in regulation of HIF by hydroxylating C-terminal asparagines (Zhang et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Zhang et al., 2010.

claim: FIH/HIF1AN has other targets besides HIF and could serve a more general function in sponges, unrelated to oxygen metabolism.
source: However, this protein has other targets (Wilkins et al., 2012) and could serve a more general function in sponges, unrelated to oxygen metabolism.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Wilkins et al., 2012 and inference about sponge biology.

claim: The absence of essential components of the HIF pathway in sponges and ctenophores suggests that these taxa are unable to modulate their transcriptional state in response to low oxygen levels in the same way as the remaining animal phyla.
source: Overall, the absence of essential components of the HIF pathway in sponges and ctenophores further suggests that these taxa are unable to modulate their transcriptional state in response to low oxygen levels, at least not in the same way as the remaining animal phyla.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the genomic data.

claim: Transcriptomes from clones of the demosponge Tethya wilhelma kept at different oxygen levels over the course of 4 days were examined.
source: To test whether sponges regulate their transcription in response to low-oxygen availability, we examined transcriptomes from clones of the demosponge Tethya wilhelma (Sarà et al., 2001) kept at different oxygen levels over the course of 4 days.
evidence: The claim describes the experimental design and cites Sarà et al., 2001 for the species.

claim: Between low-oxygen treatments (0.25–2% of modern atmospheric saturation or 0.5–4 µM O2) and high-oxygen controls (94–100% AS or 198–211 µM O2), 128 differentially expressed genes were found out of 37,000 total genes predicted in the Tethya wilhelma genome.
source: Between our low-oxygen treatments, which involved progressively lowering the oxygen concentration until it reached 0.25–2% of modern atmospheric saturation (AS) (0.5–4 µM O2 at 26°C and a salinity of 32), and our high-oxygen controls (94–100% AS or 198–211 µM O2), we found 128 differentially expressed genes (Benjamini-Hochberg corrected p-value<0.01) out of the 37,000 total genes predicted in the genome (Francis et al., 2017) (Supplementary file 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data and cites Francis et al., 2017 for the genome.

claim: None of the 128 differentially expressed genes in Tethya wilhelma under low oxygen have predicted functions related to metabolism or stress.
source: None of these differentially expressed genes have predicted functions related to metabolism or stress (based on similarity to any SwissProt protein or Amphimedon queenslandica proteins)
evidence: The claim is supported by functional annotation analysis of the differentially expressed genes.

claim: 46 of the 128 differentially expressed genes in Tethya wilhelma under low oxygen have no matches to any known protein.
source: while 46 have no matches to any known protein in our set.
evidence: The claim is supported by sequence similarity analysis.

claim: The transcriptional response of Tethya wilhelma to low oxygen contrasts sharply with HIF-mediated changes in other animals.
source: This response contrasts sharply with HIF-mediated changes in other animals and supports the assessment that sponges lack the HIF pathway, and have not independently evolved a comparable oxygen-sensing transcription factor.
evidence: The claim is based on comparison of experimental results with known responses in other animals.

claim: In the placozoan Trichoplax adhaerens, exposure to 10 µM O2 resulted in the upregulation of glycolytic enzymes, and death within 5 hr.
source: For example, in the placozoan Trichoplax adhaerens, exposure to 10 µM O2 resulted in the upregulation of glycolytic enzymes, and death within 5 hr (Loenarz et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Loenarz et al., 2011.

claim: In cnidarians, polyps and medusae of Aurelia sp.1 exhibited higher expression of HIFa after exposure to 16 µM O2 for 18 hr, relative to polyps and medusae kept under 250 µM O2 for the same length of time.
source: In cnidarians, polyps and medusae of Aurelia sp.1 exhibited higher expression of HIFa after exposure to 16 µM O2 for 18 hr, relative to polyps and medusae kept under 250 µM O2 for the same length of time (Wang et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Wang et al., 2014.

claim: After exposing Tethya wilhelma to complete anoxia in a closed, non-circulating system for 1 hr, 5981 genes were differentially expressed relative to the 4 day, high-oxygen control experiments.
source: After exposing T. wilhelma to complete anoxia in a closed, non-circulating system for 1 hr, 5981 genes were differentially expressed (Benjamini-Hochberg corrected p-value<0.01) relative to the 4 day, high-oxygen control experiments.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data.

claim: Of the 5981 differentially expressed genes under anoxia, 569 genes were differentially overexpressed (log fold change ≥ 2) and 142 genes were differentially underexpressed (log fold change ≤ −2) in treated vs. control sponges.
source: Of this set, 569 genes were differentially overexpressed (log fold change ≥ 2) and 142 genes were differentially underexpressed (log fold change ≤ −2) in treated vs. control sponges (Supplementary file 3)
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data.

claim: The differentially expressed genes under anoxia include some metabolic genes (glycogen debranching enzyme, three heme binding proteins, 10 ubiquitin ligases), implying that the sponges may be stressed by these conditions.
source: and include some metabolic genes (glycogen debranching enzyme, three heme binding proteins, 10 ubiquitin ligases), implying that the sponges may be stressed by these conditions.
evidence: The claim is supported by functional annotation of differentially expressed genes and inference about stress.

claim: Half of the differentially expressed genes under anoxia lack a reliable BLAST hit to an annotated protein.
source: As with the low-oxygen treatment, half of the differentially expressed genes lack a reliable BLAST hit to an annotated protein, making it difficult to define which biological processes are most affected.
evidence: The claim is supported by sequence similarity analysis.

claim: One of the most strongly upregulated genes under anoxia is a cryptochrome, a light-dependent regulator of bHLH-PAS proteins involved in circadian rhythms.
source: Curiously, one of the most strongly upregulated genes is a cryptochrome, a light-dependent regulator of bHLH-PAS proteins involved in circadian rhythms (Rivera et al., 2012)
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data and a citation to Rivera et al., 2012.

claim: The upregulation of cryptochrome under anoxia suggests potential for cross-talk between circadian rhythms and redox state, as seen in some vertebrates.
source: suggesting potential for cross-talk between circadian rhythms and redox state, as seen in some vertebrates (Rutter et al., 2001; Hirayama et al., 2007).
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the data and citations to Rutter et al., 2001 and Hirayama et al., 2007.

claim: All six bHLH-PAS proteins in Tethya wilhelma were upregulated to some degree under anoxia.
source: All six bHLH-PAS proteins were upregulated to some degree, whereby the log fold change was greater than one for only the HSN-like group one proteins (see Figure 2) and the ARNT homolog
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data and reference to Figure 2.

claim: It is unclear what controls the expression of bHLH-PAS proteins in Tethya wilhelma under anoxia, whether any of these proteins regulate themselves, or what the downstream targets may be.
source: although it is unclear what controls their expression, whether any of these proteins regulate themselves, or what the downstream targets may be.
evidence: The claim acknowledges the limitations of the study.

claim: The study did not explore how long Tethya wilhelma can survive complete anoxia.
source: We did not explore how long T. wilhelma can survive complete anoxia.
evidence: The claim explicitly states a limitation of the study.

claim: Metabolic function in Tethya wilhelma is unaffected by oxygen levels as low as 0.25% AS, the lowest levels observed.
source: Overall, our data suggests that metabolic function in T. wilhelma is unaffected by oxygen levels as low as 0.25% AS, the lowest levels observed
evidence: The claim is based on the transcriptome data showing minimal changes.

claim: Complete anoxia in still water induces stress in Tethya wilhelma when assayed at the mRNA level.
source: and that complete anoxia in still water induces stress -- at least when assayed at the mRNA level.
evidence: The claim is based on the transcriptome data showing many differentially expressed genes.

claim: Tethya wilhelma performs periodic full-body contractions under air-saturated oxygen levels.
source: T. wilhelma performs periodic full-body contractions under air-saturated oxygen levels (Nickel, 2004).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Nickel, 2004.

claim: No significant difference in contraction rate was observed in Tethya wilhelma under oxygen concentrations between 4 and 100% AS (8.45–211 μM O2).
source: During our 4-day experiments, we observed no significant difference in contraction rate under oxygen concentrations between 4 and 100% AS (8.45–211 μM O2) (Figure 4a, Video 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4a and Video 1.

claim: Full-body contractions in Tethya wilhelma ceased at ≤1.86% AS (3.9 µM O2).
source: Full-body contractions did cease, however, at ≤1.86% AS (3.9 µM O2) (Figure 4a).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4a.

claim: Elevated rates of oxygen uptake were observed during the contraction period in Tethya wilhelma.
source: in separate oxygen drawdown experiments, we observed elevated rates of oxygen uptake during the contraction period (Figure 4d)
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4d.

claim: The sponges may have been energetically limited under ≤1.86% AS, potentially explaining why contractions ceased.
source: We are uncertain as to why contractions ceased under these low-oxygen levels, but in separate oxygen drawdown experiments, we observed elevated rates of oxygen uptake during the contraction period (Figure 4d), potentially signifying that the sponges were energetically limited under ≤1.86% AS.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the oxygen uptake data shown in Figure 4d.

claim: The transcriptomes of the treatment and control sponges did not significantly differ (Adonis Pseudo-F = 1.6138, p=0.06).
source: However, the transcriptomes of the treatment and control sponges did not significantly differ (Figure 5a; Adonis Pseudo-F = 1.6138, p=0.06)
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of transcriptome data shown in Figure 5a.

claim: The cessation of contraction in Tethya wilhelma was not associated with any shifts in gene regulation.
source: showing that the cessation of contraction was not associated with any shifts in gene regulation.
evidence: The claim is based on the transcriptome data showing no significant differences.

claim: Local sub-contractions across the sponge surface resumed under oxygen levels as low as 0.25% AS (0.53 µM O2).
source: Furthermore, local sub-contractions across the sponge surface resumed under oxygen levels as low as 0.25% AS (0.53 µM O2).
evidence: The claim is supported by observational data.

claim: Exposure to 0.25–1.86% AS (0.53–3.9 µM O2) was not associated with any visible or transcriptional indicators of stress or death in Tethya wilhelma, suggesting that T. wilhelma remains viable under these levels.
source: In summary, independently of whether these sponges were unable to contract, or no longer needed to -- perhaps to regulate their internal redox balance, as seen in the demosponge Geodia barretti (Hoffmann et al., 2005) -- exposure to 0.25–1.86% AS (0.53–3.9 µM O2) was not associated with any visible or transcriptional indicators of stress or death, suggesting that T. wilhelma remains viable under these levels.
evidence: The claim is based on experimental observations and transcriptome data, with a citation to Hoffmann et al., 2005.

claim: The HIF pathway evolved only once in animals, after the last common ancestor (LCA) of Bilateria + Cnidaria + Placozoa split from sponges and ctenophores.
source: As shown here, the HIF pathway evolved only once in animals, after the last common ancestor (LCA) of Bilateria + Cnidaria + Placozoa split from sponges and ctenophores.
evidence: The claim is based on phylogenetic inference from the comparative genomics data.

claim: The HIF pathway is not a universal metazoan trait.
source: Therefore, the HIF pathway is not a universal metazoan trait, as previously thought (Loenarz et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is based on the findings of this study and contrasts with a previous claim by Loenarz et al., 2011.

claim: Sponges and ctenophores likely detect and respond to oxygen availability at the cellular level via other mechanisms, such as the allosteric regulation of heme proteins, or changes in the conductance of O2-sensitive ion channels.
source: While sponges and ctenophores lack the capacity to sense oxygen via transcriptional regulators like HIF, they likely detect and respond to oxygen availability at the cellular level via other mechanisms, such as the allosteric regulation of heme proteins, or changes in the conductance of O2-sensitive ion channels (Chandel and Schumacker, 2000).
evidence: The claim is based on inference and a citation to Chandel and Schumacker, 2000.

claim: At the mitochondrial level, electron transport and oxidative phosphorylation cease under anoxia.
source: At the mitochondrial level, electron transport and oxidative phosphorylation cease under anoxia
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge of mitochondrial biochemistry.

claim: Hypoxia reversibly lowers the maximum reaction rate (Vmax) of the cytochrome C oxidase, thereby lowering the mitochondrial redox state and promoting the production of reactive oxygen species.
source: while hypoxia reversibly lowers the maximum reaction rate (Vmax) of the cytochrome C oxidase, thereby lowering the mitochondrial redox state and promoting the production of reactive oxygen species (Chandel and Schumacker, 2000).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Chandel and Schumacker, 2000.

claim: Cytochrome C is inhibited by hydrogen sulfide.
source: Cytochrome C is also inhibited by hydrogen sulfide (Powell and Somero, 1986; Cooper and Brown, 2008)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Powell and Somero, 1986 and Cooper and Brown, 2008.

claim: Hydrogen sulfide may serve as an indirect mechanism of oxygen detection, as environmental or metabolic sulfide can accumulate under anoxia and is removed in the mitochondria by a series of O2-dependent reactions to produce sulfate.
source: which may serve as an indirect mechanism of oxygen detection, as environmental or metabolic sulfide can accumulate under anoxia and is removed in the mitochondria by a series of O2-dependent reactions to produce sulfate.
evidence: The claim is based on inference about biochemical pathways.

claim: Most of the enzymes involved in the sulfide-removal pathway are found in all non-bilaterian groups.
source: Most of the enzymes involved in this sulfide-removal pathway are found in all non-bilaterian groups (Figure 1—figure supplement 1)
evidence: The claim is supported by comparative genomics data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: The absence of oxygen can be more universally detected among animals at the mitochondrial level through the presence of sulfide.
source: implying that these mechanisms are conserved, and that the absence of oxygen can be more universally detected among animals at the mitochondrial level through the presence of sulfide.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the genomic data.

claim: The combination of the bHLH and PAS domains was found only in metazoans and the single-celled eukaryote C. owczarzaki.
source: However, the combination of the bHLH and PAS domains was found only in metazoans and the single-celled eukaryote C. owczarzaki, showing that this domain combination pre-dates the origin of animals (Sebé-Pedrós et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by comparative genomics data and a citation to Sebé-Pedrós et al., 2012.

claim: The bHLH-PAS domain combination pre-dates the origin of animals.
source: showing that this domain combination pre-dates the origin of animals (Sebé-Pedrós et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the presence of bHLH-PAS in C. owczarzaki and a citation to Sebé-Pedrós et al., 2012.

claim: PAS domains have binding pockets capable of holding small molecules, such as heme in the case of fixL, and flavin for WC1.
source: PAS domains have binding pockets capable of holding small molecules, such as heme in the case of fixL, and flavin for WC1.
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge of PAS domain structure and function.

claim: Recent crystal structures of several mouse bHLH-PAS proteins suggest potential binding pockets in both PAS domains, as well as the dimerization interface.
source: Recent crystal structures of several mouse bHLH-PAS proteins suggest potential binding pockets in both PAS domains, as well as the dimerization interface (Wu et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Wu et al., 2016.

claim: bHLH-PAS proteins uninvolved in the HIF pathway could be indirectly affected by the redox state of ligands, such as flavins.
source: Thus, even bHLH-PAS proteins uninvolved in the HIF pathway could be indirectly affected by the redox state of ligands, such as flavins.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from structural data.

claim: The presence of oxidized or reduced factors, such as FAD or NADH, could affect dimerization of bHLH-PAS proteins, which may affect downstream transcription.
source: Conceivably, the presence of oxidized or reduced factors, such as FAD or NADH, could affect dimerization, which may affect downstream transcription.
evidence: The claim is speculative, based on inference from structural and biochemical knowledge.

claim: Euplokamis dunlapae belongs to the sister group to all other ctenophores.
source: Interestingly, E. dunlapae belongs to the sister group to all other ctenophores (Simion et al., 2015)
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Simion et al., 2015.

claim: The homologs of the E. dunlapae bHLH-PAS protein in other ctenophores lack the ODD motif.
source: yet the homologs of the E. dunlapae protein in other ctenophores lack the ODD motif
evidence: The claim is supported by sequence analysis.

claim: The function of the E. dunlapae bHLH-PAS protein is unlikely to be the same as HIFa, or at least cannot involve the same binding partners, since EGL9 or VHL were not found in any available ctenophore transcriptome or genome.
source: Since we were unable to find EGL9 or VHL in any available ctenophore transcriptome or genome, the function of the E. dunlapae bHLH-PAS protein is unlikely be the same as HIFa, or at least cannot involve the same binding partners.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the absence of key HIF pathway components.

claim: Additional experimental investigation and genome sequencing on E. dunlapae and closely related species are needed to resolve the question of oxygen regulation in ctenophores.
source: Overall, additional experimental investigation and genome sequencing -- particular on E. dunlapae and closely related species -- are still needed to resolve the question of oxygen regulation in ctenophores.
evidence: The claim acknowledges the limitations of the current study.

claim: The majority of phylogenetic analyses recovered either sponges or ctenophores as sister to all other animals, but agreed on the position of Placozoa as the sister to a Cnidaria + Bilateria clade.
source: The majority of analyses recovered either sponges or ctenophores as sister to all other animals, but agreed on the position of Placozoa as the sister to a Cnidaria + Bilateria clade.
evidence: The claim summarizes the state of phylogenetic knowledge.

claim: Most components of the HIF pathway are absent in both sponges and ctenophores, with all the components present in the clade of Bilateria + Cnidaria + Placozoa.
source: Most components of the HIF pathway are absent in both sponges and ctenophores, with all the components present in the clade of Bilateria + Cnidaria + Placozoa.
evidence: The claim is based on the comparative genomics data.

claim: The acquisition of the HIF pathway is independent of the phylogenetic position of ctenophores, as it occurred after the divergence of both ctenophores and sponges from all other animals.
source: Therefore, the acquisition of the HIF pathway is independent of the phylogenetic position of ctenophores, as it occurred after the divergence of both ctenophores and sponges from all other animals (Figure 6).
evidence: The claim is based on phylogenetic inference and is illustrated in Figure 6.

claim: Recent molecular clock estimates suggest that all non-bilaterian phyla emerged in rapid succession between 850 and 820 Ma, and that this timing was independent of the phylogenetic position of ctenophores.
source: Furthermore, recent molecular clock estimates suggest that all non-bilaterian phyla emerged in rapid succession between 850 and 820 Ma, and that this timing was independent of the phylogenetic position of ctenophores (Dohrmann and Wörheide, 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Dohrmann and Wörheide, 2017.

claim: Sponges are found at oxygen concentrations as low as ~3–8 µM O2 along the lower boundary of the Peruvian oxygen-minimum zone (OMZ).
source: Sponges are found at oxygen concentrations as low as ~3–8 µM O2 along the lower boundary of the Peruvian oxygen-minimum zone (OMZ) (Mosch et al., 2012)
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Mosch et al., 2012.

claim: Sponges are found at ~4 µM O2 on the lower summit of the Volcano 7 Seamount, Eastern Tropical Pacific.
source: and at ~4 µM O2 on the lower summit of the Volcano 7 Seamount, Eastern Tropical Pacific (Levin, 2003).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Levin, 2003.

claim: Natural sponge populations live at oxygen concentrations approaching those under which normal transcription was observed in T. wilhelma (<4 µM O2).
source: Therefore, natural sponge populations live at oxygen concentrations approaching those under which we observed normal transcription in T. wilhelma (<4 µM O2).
evidence: The claim is based on comparison of field observations with experimental data.

claim: Marine sponges in Lake Lough Hyne, Ireland can apparently endure anoxia during summer thermal stratification.
source: For example, marine sponges in Lake Lough Hyne, Ireland can apparently endure anoxia during summer thermal stratification (Bell and Barnes, 2000)
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Bell and Barnes, 2000.

claim: Freshwater sponge gemmules can survive anoxia for months.
source: and freshwater sponge gemmules can survive anoxia for months (Reiswig and Miller, 1998).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Reiswig and Miller, 1998.

claim: At least some sponge species can establish themselves under low-oxygen levels in nature, despite lacking the HIF pathway.
source: Therefore, at least some sponge species can establish themselves under low-oxygen levels in nature, despite lacking the HIF pathway.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from field observations and genomic data.

claim: Ctenophores are well known for inhabiting low-oxygen environments.
source: Ctenophores, the only other animal phylum predicted to lack the HIF pathway, are well known for inhabiting low-oxygen environments (Purcell et al., 2001).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Purcell et al., 2001.

claim: In the OMZ of the North Chilean coast, the highest abundance of ctenophores (as determined through rRNA abundance) was found at oxygen levels of 6.1 µM O2, defining the upper oxic-anoxic interface.
source: For example, in the OMZ of the North Chilean coast, the highest abundance of ctenophores (as determined through rRNA abundance) was found at oxygen levels of 6.1 µM O2, defining the upper oxic-anoxic interface (Parris et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Parris et al., 2014.

claim: Ctenophores were found, although at lower abundance, in the anoxic core of the OMZ in the North Chilean coast.
source: Ctenophores were also found, although at lower abundance, in the anoxic core of the OMZ (Parris et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Parris et al., 2014.

claim: In the Eastern Tropical North Pacific, plankton nets collected the highest abundance of ctenophores in OMZ waters with oxygen concentrations as low as 3–30 μM.
source: Similarly, in the Eastern Tropical North Pacific, plankton nets collected the highest abundance of ctenophores in OMZ waters with oxygen concentrations as low as 3–30 μM (Beatteay, 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Beatteay, 2012.

claim: Ctenophores have low metabolic oxygen demands.
source: Overall, ctenophores have low metabolic oxygen demands, and feature most metabolically active cells in direct contact with the environment (Thuesen et al., 2005)
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Thuesen et al., 2005.

claim: Most metabolically active cells in ctenophores are in direct contact with the environment, thereby facilitating life under low-oxygen.
source: and feature most metabolically active cells in direct contact with the environment (Thuesen et al., 2005), thereby facilitating life under low-oxygen (Purcell et al., 2001).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Thuesen et al., 2005 and Purcell et al., 2001.

claim: Cnidarians have similar distributions along modern oxygen gradients as ctenophores.
source: Cnidarians, which unlike ctenophores possess the HIF pathway (Loenarz et al., 2011; Wang et al., 2014), have similar distributions along modern oxygen gradients (Purcell et al., 2001; Parris et al., 2014)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Loenarz et al., 2011, Wang et al., 2014, Purcell et al., 2001, and Parris et al., 2014.

claim: Adaptation to life in low-oxygen environments is not predicated on the possession of HIF.
source: demonstrating that adaptation to life in low-oxygen environments is not predicated on the possession of HIF.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the similar distributions of cnidarians and ctenophores.

claim: Placozoans appear to be relatively sensitive to low-oxygen conditions, as seen in T. adhaerens, which dies after 5 hr of exposure to 10 µM O2.
source: Despite their morphological simplicity, placozoans appear to be relatively sensitive to low-oxygen conditions, as seen in T. adhaerens, which dies after 5 hr of exposure to 10 µM O2 (Loenarz et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Loenarz et al., 2011.

claim: Placozoans are found in shallow coastal waters <20 m deep.
source: In nature, placozoans are found in shallow coastal waters <20 m deep (Eitel et al., 2013)
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Eitel et al., 2013.

claim: Placozoans have not been reported from any low-oxygen systems.
source: and have not, at least to our knowledge, been reported from any low-oxygen systems.
evidence: The claim is based on the authors' knowledge of the literature.

claim: Placozoans phagocytose microbial prey via their upper epithelia, and feed through external digestion and osmotrophy via their lower epithelia.
source: Placozoans phagocytose microbial prey via their upper epithelia, and feed through external digestion and osmotrophy via their lower epithelia (Eitel et al., 2013)
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Eitel et al., 2013.

claim: Placozoans occupy trophic levels predicted to be supported in low-oxygen environments.
source: and therefore occupy trophic levels predicted to be supported in low-oxygen environments (Fenchel and Finlay, 1995).
evidence: The claim is based on inference and a citation to Fenchel and Finlay, 1995.

claim: Most filter-feeding sponges subsist on small microbial prey and dissolved organics, and therefore occupy the same trophic levels as placozoans.
source: Indeed, most filter-feeding sponges (in contrast to carnivorous sponges) also subsist on small microbial prey and dissolved organics, and therefore occupy the same trophic levels as placozoans (Mills and Canfield, 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Mills and Canfield, 2017.

claim: The sensitivity of placozoans to low-oxygen conditions is difficult to explain in terms of their body plan and trophic style.
source: The sensitivity of placozoans to low-oxygen conditions is therefore difficult to explain in terms of their body plan and trophic style.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the comparison of placozoans with sponges.

claim: All metazoans outside of ctenophores and sponges are predicted to have the HIF pathway.
source: All metazoans outside of ctenophores and sponges are predicted to have the HIF pathway (Loenarz et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is based on the findings of this study and a citation to Loenarz et al., 2011.

claim: Similar mechanisms of transcriptional regulation by oxygen-dependent degradation of transcription factors have been identified in fungi.
source: Outside of animals, similar mechanisms of transcriptional regulation by oxygen-dependent degradation of transcription factors have been identified in fungi (Lee et al., 2009)
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Lee et al., 2009.

claim: Similar mechanisms of transcriptional regulation by oxygen-dependent degradation of transcription factors have been identified in the social amoeba Dictyostelium.
source: the social amoeba Dictyostelium (van der Wel et al., 2005)
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to van der Wel et al., 2005.

claim: Similar mechanisms of transcriptional regulation by oxygen-dependent degradation of transcription factors have been identified in plants.
source: and plants (Licausi et al., 2011)
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Licausi et al., 2011.

claim: Oxygen-dependent transcriptional control systems in fungi, Dictyostelium, and plants all use different protein components.
source: although these systems all use different protein components.
evidence: The claim is based on knowledge from the cited literature.

claim: Oxygen-dependent transcriptional control has evolved convergently in multiple multicellular eukaryotic lineages.
source: Overall, it appears that oxygen-dependent transcriptional control has evolved convergently in multiple multicellular eukaryotic lineages.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the comparative data across eukaryotes.

claim: The ancestral absence of the HIF pathway in metazoans suggests that stem-group metazoans and the metazoan LCA did not regulate their transcription in response to oxygen availability.
source: The ancestral absence of the HIF pathway in metazoans suggests that stem-group metazoans and the metazoan LCA did not regulate their transcription in response to oxygen availability.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the phylogenetic distribution of HIF.

claim: Animals most likely originated prior to the establishment of modern atmospheric oxygen levels and the permanent oxygenation of the deep ocean.
source: While it is unclear how much oxygen crown-group animals ancestrally required (Mills and Canfield, 2014), animals most likely originated prior to the establishment of modern atmospheric oxygen levels and the permanent oxygenation of the deep ocean (Lenton and Daines, 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Mills and Canfield, 2014 and Lenton and Daines, 2017.

claim: The earliest metazoans could have functioned and respired under environmental oxygen concentrations as low as 0.25% of modern atmospheric saturation, and perhaps even lower.
source: In this case, the ancestral absence of HIF in animals suggests that the earliest metazoans could have functioned and respired under environmental oxygen concentrations as low as 0.25% of modern atmospheric saturation, and perhaps even lower
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the experimental data on T. wilhelma and the phylogenetic distribution of HIF.

claim: The earliest metazoans did not need to respond to low-oxygen availability at the transcriptional level.
source: and did not need to respond to low-oxygen availability at the transcriptional level.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the absence of HIF in the metazoan LCA.

claim: The last common ancestor of animals lacked the HIF pathway.
source: Since sponges and ctenophores are likely sister to all remaining animal phyla, the last common ancestor of extant animals likely lacked the HIF pathway as well.
evidence: The claim is based on phylogenetic inference from the absence of HIF in sponges and ctenophores.

claim: The marine sponge Tethya wilhelma maintains normal transcription under oxygen levels down to 0.25% of modern atmospheric saturation.
source: Laboratory experiments show that the marine sponge Tethya wilhelma maintains normal transcription under oxygen levels down to 0.25% of modern atmospheric saturation, the lowest levels we investigated, consistent with the predicted absence of HIF or any other HIF-like pathway.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data.

claim: The last common ancestor of all living animals could have metabolized aerobically under very low environmental oxygen concentrations.
source: Thus, the last common ancestor of all living animals could have metabolized aerobically under very low environmental oxygen concentrations.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the experimental data and phylogenetic analysis.
